 1                        I.      WITNESS IDENTIFICATION

 2   Q.   Please state your name and business address.

 3   A.   My name is Todd A. Wehner. My business address is 414 Nicollet Mall,

 4        Minneapolis, Minnesota 55401.

 5   Q.   On whose behalf are you testifying in this proceeding?

 6   A.   I am filing testimony on behalf of Southwestern Public Service Company, a New

 7        Mexico corporation (“SPS”) and a wholly-owned electric utility subsidiary of Xcel

 8        Energy Inc.

 9   Q.   Are you the same Todd A. Wehner who filed direct testimony on behalf of SPS

10        in this case?

11   A.   Yes.

 1             II.     ASSIGNMENT AND SUMMARY OF TESTIMONY

 2   Q.   What is your assignment in this testimony?

 3   A.   My testimony supports the reasonableness of the terms of the Comprehensive

 4        Stipulation (“Stipulation”) regarding SPS’s capital structure.

 5   Q.   Please summarize your testimony and overall recommendations.

 6   A.   I recommend the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission (“Commission”)

 7        approve the Stipulation in its entirety. My testimony below specifically supports

 8        the following aspect of the Stipulation: capital structure of 54.7 percent equity and

 9        long-term debt of 45.3 percent.

10   Q.   Do any other witnesses provide testimony related to those issues?

11   A.   Yes. SPS witness Ann E. Bulkley is presenting testimony regarding return on

12        equity.

 1            III.       REASONABLENESS OF THE STIPULATION CAPITAL
 2                                      STRUCTURE

 3   Q.   What was SPS’s actual capital structure during the period July 1, 2024,

 4        through June 30, 2025 (“Base Period”)?

 5   A.   SPS’s actual capital structure during the Base Period (July 1, 2024, through June

 6        30, 2025) was 54.76 percent equity and 45.24 percent long-term debt. This is

 7        generally consistent with the Stipulation capital structure.

 8   Q.   Is the agreed capital structure provided in the Stipulation reasonable?

 9   A.   Yes. The agreed equity ratio of 54.7 percent equity and 45.3 percent long-term debt

10        is reasonable for several reasons. The Stipulation capital structure is unchanged

11        from SPS’s current authorized capital structure. 1 The Stipulation’s capital structure

12        includes a six basis point reduction to the Base Period equity component (and a

13        corresponding six basis point increase in the Base Period debt component), but is

14        generally consistent with the prior Commission-approved capital structure for SPS.

15        Second, the Stipulation’s capital structure is approximately equal to the ratio of debt

16        and equity capital used to finance the Base Period capital additions included in the

17        cost of service presented in this rate proceeding. Third, as Ms. Bulkley discusses

 1        in her direct testimony, this capital structure is within the range of the capital

 2        structures of the Utility Proxy Group’s operating subsidiary companies. 2

 3   Q.   What are SPS’s current credit ratings?

 4   A.   SPS currently has corporate ratings of Baa2/BBB/BBB, senior secured ratings of

 5        A3/A-/A-, and commercial paper ratings of P-2/A-2/F2 (Moody’s/S&P/Fitch), 3

 6        primarily due to heightened business and regulatory risk as compared to similarly-

 7        rated companies. 4 Lower credit ratings are seen as riskier and therefore investors

 8        demand a higher spread in order to compensate for the higher level of risk. This

 9        results in a higher cost of debt that is directly passed through to customers.

10   Q.   Do Commission decisions regarding rate case settlements impact SPS’s access

11        to credit on reasonable terms?

12   A.   Yes. The settlement of SPS’s most recent New Mexico rate case (Case No.

13        22-00286-UT) was seen as credit positive by the rating agencies 5 and was a

14        supportive step in improving perceptions of New Mexico’s regulatory impact on

15        SPS’s business risk. Lowering SPS’s cost of debt is very important, given future

 1            capital needs. 6 In order to realize this lower cost of debt, capital market investors

 2            need to see consistency and a stable commitment to maintaining a supportive

 3            regulatory environment in New Mexico. Approval of this Stipulation would be a

 4            supportive indicator of the Commission’s commitment to continuing momentum of

 5            consistent and supportive regulatory decisions, which would be viewed favorably

 6            by rating agencies and capital market investors alike.

 7   Q.       Does the Stipulation in this proceeding offer the opportunity to assist in

 8            maintaining SPS’s financial integrity?

 9   A.       On the whole, yes. While a 54.7 percent equity ratio and traditional funding of

10            Allowance for Funds Used During Construction produces forecasted credit metrics

11            that are slightly above the downgrade threshold, 7 the overall Stipulation and the

12            Commission’s approval of and the terms of the Stipulation would be an indication

13            of continued positive momentum in reducing regulatory risk in New Mexico. 8

14            Although the Stipulation reflects a reduction to SPS’s requested revenue

 1        requirement, it is not likely to enable SPS to recover its former credit rating, and it

 2        does not leave much financial flexibility as SPS continues investment. The

 3        Stipulation does help address business (regulatory) risk and therefore is reasonably

 4        supportive of SPS’s financial integrity. This is a direct benefit to SPS customers as

 5        SPS would be better positioned to provide safe, clean, and reliable electric service

 6        to its customers at a reasonable cost through all economic conditions.

 7   Q.   What are the implications of a decision by the Commission to reject the

 8        Stipulation?

 9   A.   As explained in my Direct Testimony, regulatory frameworks critically influence

10        the financial performance of utilities. Regulatory risk is a pivotal determinant in

11        credit rating outcomes and is therefore subject to substantial scrutiny by rating

12        agencies. 9 That scrutiny considers (1) the legal foundation for utility regulation,

13        (2) the ratemaking policies and procedures that determine how well the utility is

14        afforded the opportunity to earn a reasonable return with reasonable cash flow, and

15        (3) the history of regulatory behavior by commissions applying those laws, policies

 1        and procedures. Then, they examine the mechanics of regulation, particularly the

 2        rate-setting process. 10

 3        As discussed by SPS witness Zoë E. Lees, the Stipulation before the Commission

 4        is the result of extensive negotiations among numerous parties representing diverse

 5        stakeholder interests. The Stipulation is the product of a compromise among well-

 6        represented parties that provides SPS with some, but not all, of its revenue

 7        requirement. The fact that all parties were able to negotiate a settlement, with

 8        Commission Staff only in opposition to portions of the settlement, is itself credit

 9        positive, in that it demonstrates constructive outcomes are possible in New Mexico.

10        The rejection of this Stipulation would likely signal a non-supportive regulatory

11        environment, which could halt momentum on recent improvements in New Mexico

12        regulatory risk, and put additional pressure on SPS’s credit ratings and financial

13        integrity.

14   Q.   Does this conclude your pre-filed testimony in support of the Stipulation?

15   A.   Yes, it does.
